summary:
YAKU (Quechua for “water”) is a free, open web app that estimates how much water mountain wetlands store, and how that reserve changes, using the NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar. Mountains supply up to 60% of the world’s annual freshwater flows, yet the water held by high-Andean peatlands (bofedales) is rarely measured, and clouds hide them from optical satellites when it matters most.

Answering the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, YAKU turns complex SAR data into decisions. It downloads calibrated NISAR GCOV products from ASF DAAC, masks terrain with the Copernicus DEM, classifies open water and saturated wetland from HH and HV backscatter, and converts moisture into cubic metres, with a daily water balance from NASA POWER. Users get maps, a reserve traffic light, a live monitor and a one-click PDF report, tailored to communities, public agencies, researchers and mining companies.

In our pilot, the Cachi River headwaters in Ayacucho, Peru, six real NISAR images (June-October 2026) showed about 20 million m³ of seasonal change. These preliminary figures are being calibrated at the Apacheta wetland. The same open code works for any mountain wetland on Earth.

Bofedales are the water reserves of the mountains: the reserves of life. With NASA’s support, YAKU can grow, reach every mountain range and become a tool against climate change, helping the world manage its water better when it is needed most.
details:
What it does
YAKU (Quechua for “water”) estimates how much water mountain wetlands store and how that reserve changes over time, using the NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar. High-Andean peatlands (bofedales) act as sponges: they hold rain and release it in the dry season, sustaining rivers and the cities downstream. Their water is rarely measured, and clouds hide them from optical satellites in the rainy season. NISAR’s 24 cm radar sees through clouds, day and night, and revisits every 12 days, so YAKU can turn its echoes into cubic metres of water.

How it works

  1. Download: calibrated NISAR GCOV products (HH and HV) from NASA’s ASF DAAC, with a free Earthdata account.
  2. Clean: multilooking to 60 m pixels and conversion to decibels.
  3. Terrain: the Copernicus 30 m DEM keeps only land above 3,800 m with slopes under 15%.
  4. Classify: open water when HH is below an Otsu threshold (about -16 dB) and HV below -20 dB; saturated wetland when HH is at or above -9 dB on at least 30% of dates.
  5. Volume: ponds + an active peat layer whose moisture changes + deep saturated peat, plus a daily water balance (rain minus evapotranspiration) from NASA POWER.
    Processing runs automatically in the cloud with GitHub Actions. The results feed YAKU App.

Data flow
NISAR satellite (L-band, every 12 days) → ASF DAAC (GCOV, free Earthdata account) → GitHub Actions (Python: clean, terrain mask, classify) → volume in m³ + NASA POWER daily balance → YAKU App (maps, traffic light, PDF report, alerts)

What users get
YAKU App shows the wetland map with radar layers (water and wetland, moisture, false colour, HH, HV), playback of every NISAR date, comparison between two dates, a cross-section of the wetland “sponge” in m³, a live monitor with a green/amber/red reserve traffic light, a one-click PDF report and an editable business model. It adapts its advice to four profiles: communities, public agencies, researchers and mining companies. It is free, works in English and Spanish, installs on any phone and works offline.

Pilot results (Cachi River headwaters, Ayacucho, Peru)
The Cachi River headwaters are the main water source of Ayacucho city (2013 inventory: 883 wetlands, 14,500 ha).
Indicator | Value
NISAR images | 6 (Jun 19 – Oct 29, 2026), 0 lost to clouds
Orbit / coverage | 075-A / 87% of the area per pass
Processing time | 6.5 minutes in the cloud
Seasonal change in stored water | ≈ 20 million m³ (≈ 8,000 Olympic pools)
Equivalent | ≈ 540 days of water for a city of 250,000
Wetland area detected | 23,525 ha (2013 inventory: 14,500 ha → calibrating)
Live monitor (Nov 12, 2026) | active-layer reserve 47%, ≈ 11.9 million m³
NISAR detected 1.6 times the 2013 inventory, so we are calibrating the wetland threshold at the Apacheta control point (4,210 m) with low-cost PVC piezometers before publishing final figures.

Benefits and impact
Mountains supply up to 60% of the world’s annual freshwater flows, and about two billion people depend on mountain water (UN World Water Development Report 2025). YAKU gives water utilities, agencies, mining companies and herding communities a measured volume instead of a guess, helping them prioritise conservation, plan for drought and protect peat that stores both water and carbon. It supports SDGs 6, 13, 15 and 17.

Business model (plans)
User | What they get | Price
Communities | Traffic light on the phone, offline | Free
Researchers | Time series, open code, data export | Free
Public agencies and water utilities | Indicators to prioritise investment and drought plans | US$ 5,000/year
Mining companies | Water baseline and 12-day monitoring | US$ 15,000/year
Mining Premium | + field calibration, custom alerts, monthly reports | US$ 20,000/year
Services | Calibration, training, custom reports | US$ 3,000 each

Financial projection (US$, illustrative and editable in YAKU App)
Year | Revenue | Costs | Result
2027 | 31,000 | 22,800 | +8,200
2028 | 80,000 | 44,700 | +35,300
2029 | 140,000 | 73,800 | +66,200
Cumulative result in 3 years: about +US$ 110,000. Revenue includes grants of US$ 15,000 (2027) and US$ 10,000 (2028); without them the project breaks even in 2028. Technology cost: US$ 0.

Sustainability
Technical: same open code for any site; NASA data, cloud processing and hosting at zero cost.
Financial: paid plans for the largest water users fund free access for communities (cross-subsidy); a lean team grows only with clients.
Social: trained community members read low-cost PVC piezometers, creating local jobs and reducing trips to 4,000 m.
Environmental: protecting peat protects dry-season water and stored carbon.

Scaling roadmap
Phase | Time | Where
Pilot | 0–6 months | Peru, Cachi River: field calibration and first alerts
National | 6–18 months | Ayacucho and other Peruvian regions
Andean | 18–36 months | Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, Chile, Argentina, Venezuela
Global | 36+ months | Himalaya (Nepal), Alps (Switzerland), Rockies (USA), adding RADARSAT and SAOCOM

Tools and technologies
Data: NISAR GCOV (ASF DAAC), NASA Earthdata and CMR, NASA POWER, Copernicus DEM GLO-30, NASA ARSET training, NISAR Data User Guide.
Software: Python (processing scripts), GitHub Actions (cloud processing), HTML, CSS and JavaScript (YAKU App and YAKU Web, installable as a Progressive Web App), GitHub Pages and Vercel (hosting).
Hardware for validation: PVC piezometers and two automatic water-level loggers per site.

How it is creative
YAKU converts radar backscatter, a signal few people can read, into the unit that decision-makers use: cubic metres of water. It uses NISAR’s L-band and its 12-day revisit to follow a water reserve through the season, and it explains the physics with plain diagrams and a traffic light anyone can understand. The same open code works for any mountain wetland on Earth: enter coordinates, altitude and area.

Factors our team considered
Scientific honesty: NISAR GCOV is still a provisional product and the dB thresholds are heuristic, so all volumes are labelled as estimates until field calibration.
Access: free for communities and researchers, plain language, two languages, offline use.
Team: Jaime Joseph Mañuico Mendoza (CEO: leadership, partnerships and business model) and Noemi Justina Tomaylla Berrocal (Project Manager: planning, coordination and fieldwork), with work areas in hydrology, SAR remote sensing, software development and community partnerships.

Call to action
Bofedales are the water reserves of the mountains: the reserves of life. With NASA’s support, YAKU can grow, reach every mountain range and become a tool against climate change, helping the world manage its water better when it is needed most.
